2. Opposite party No. 1 as appellant filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-empting 30 decimals of land of plot No. 887 In Khatian No. 205 of Mouja South Alipur; Feni District, Noakhali on the averment that the applicant was co share of the holding by inheritance and Opp. party No. 2 Abo Tayeb sold the case and to the petitioner opposite party who was a stranger by kabala dated 8-9-69 for a consideration of Tk. 3000.00 No notice of transfer was served upon the applicant who came to know of the transfer for the first time in the month of February, 1975. Thereafter, the petitioner obtained certified copy and filed the application for pre-emption on depositing consideration and compensation. The application was opposed by opposite party No 1 who is petitioner here contending inter alia, that the Pre-emptor-applicant was aware of the transfer for the last 6 rear and the application was hopelessly time-barred on these pleadings two issues were raised before the learned Munsif which are as follows:- 

 4. Mr. M. A Rouf has contended that the appellate court has failed to appreciate the evidence adduced by the parties in its proper perspective and has come to an erroneous finding as to the petitioner's case of the date of knowledge of the transfer and erroneously concluded that the application was not time barred and has acted with material irregularity In the exercise of his jurisdiction and as such his judgment cannot be sustained. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, on the other hand, has contended that the question to on what day the petitioner had acquired knowledge was a question of fact and it was concluded by the finding arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge who was the final court of fact and this cannot be questioned before this  Court. I have perused the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge and the evidence on record. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that the petitioner has stated in his deposition that he came to know of the transfer in the month of February. 1976 from Mr. Nurul Amin, father of O.P. 2. He also found that P.W. 2 Abdur Rahim corroborated this story. Mr. Rouf has contended that Natal Amin who was the source of information of the petitioner has not been examined and in the absence of the evidence of Nurul Amin it could not be said that the petitioner has proved the date of knowledge as pleaded by him. I am unable to accept the contention of the learned Advocate. The learned Subordinate Judge would be absolutely within his jurisdiction if he would have relied on even the testimony of the petitioner but in this case he found that there was a corroborative evidence supplied by P.W. 2. I am unable to accept the contention that there has been any illegality or material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction while learned Subordinate Judge made a finding that the petitioner came to know about the transfer in February, 1975 This finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is not therefore, subject to interference by this Court. 

 5. Next point that Mr. M A. Rouf has urged that the order of the learned sub-ordinate Judge was illegal and erroneous inasmuch as there was no finding that the pre-emptor  was a bonafide cultivator and he had less than 100 bighas of land as required under sections 90 and 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr. Rouf has placed the case of Nayeb Ali and others. Vs. Aktar Rahman and others reported In 29 D.L.R. 153 decided by a Single Bench of this Court. It appears that the learned Single Judge has arrived at his decision relying on the case of Satya Ranjan Halder and others Vs. Surendra Nath Das and others reported in (1961) 13 D.L.R page.338 decided by a Division Bench. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman has relied on another Single Bench decision. Abdur Rahman Vs Baser Ali and others reported in (1969) 21 D.L.R. 599. I would first of all refer to the Division Bench case reported in 13 D.L.R. 338. la that case it was held that before a person was entitled to get pre-emption, he had to prove all the requirements under section 96 of the Act. In that case, it was found that the opposite party in the written objection definitely asserted that the petitioner was owner in pension of land of more than 100 bighas. In the 21 D.L.R case, Mr. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J. sitting in single bench distinguished that case from the case of the Division Bench on the ground that in that case before him there was no averment that the opposite party No. 1 had so much land that if the preempted lard be added to It the quantity of laud in his possession would exceed the prescribed quantity of land permissible under the law. The learned Judge observed that no such question appears to have been raised in the courts below nor any objection was taken in the case but In the Division Bench case the objection was specifically taken and it was not proved otherwise. Thus, disturbing facts of the case before him from the facts of the case of the Division Bench Mr. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J. held that principle of law enunciated in the Division Bench case did not apply to his case in 29 D.L.R. (Dac) 153 Mr. Ranadhir Sen, J. held that in the absence of a finding That the pre-emptor is a person to whom transfer of the holding or a portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under sec.90 the application for pre-emption is bound to fall. I have given my anxious consideration to the ratio decidendi of the Division Bench ease which has been followed in both the subsequent Single Bench cases. The Division Bench based its decision on an Interpretation of the proviso to sub section (I) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which reads as follows: 

 "In suit in which Issues have been framed the court shall state its findings or decision, with the reasons thereof upon each separate issue, unless the finding on any one or more of the issues is sufficient for the decision of the suit." 

 6. In view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure this rule is also applicable in all proceedings before Civil Court including a proceeding under section 96 of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The rules of pleading and the rules as to no what points the court shall record findings are the same in a civil proceeding as in a suit. In the case before me, the petitioner has categorically asserted in paragraph 5 of the plaint that if the petitioners application for preemption be allowed, the provisions of P.O. 98 of 1972 would not be contravened. It may be recalled that P.O. 98 of 1972 prescribed a ceiling of 100 bighas of land that may be owned and held by a family. This averment of the petitioner has not been denied by the opposite party in his written objection. By the rules of construction of pleading, this averment of the petitioner mast be damned to have been admitted by the opposite party and the parties could not be said to be at issue on this point. I am of considered opinion that in the case of this nature no duty is cast upon the court to record a finding that the pre-emptor is a person to whom the transfer of the holding or the portion or share thereof at the cam may be, can be made under section 90 of the Act. In the Division Bench case, the opposite party, in their written objection filed In the lower court, definitely asserted that the respondent petitioner is owner in possession of land of more that 100 bighas and denied the allegation of the respondent. The present case is, therefore, distinguishable from the Division Bench Case. The facts of the present case are rather similar to the facts of the case reported In 21 D.L.R 599 which was also distinguished from the Division Bench case. The absence of any finding recorded by the court below that the pre-emptor was a person whose application for preemption, if allowed, would not contravene the prescribed ceiling, does not, in the instant case, call for a dismissal of the application for preemption. From the pleading, it can be gathered that no such contravention would occur and, as such, no dismissal is warranted. 

 7. The next question that requires consideration is whether the absence of finding by the court below that the pre-emptor was bonefide cultivator vitiates their judgments and whether such absence of finding dis-entitles the applicant, as contended by Mr. Rouf, to an order of pre-emption. From a reading of paragraph 2 of the plaint, it appears that the petitioner averred that he used to possess was share in the subject joie through Nurul Amin who was his bargadar. In section 82(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act— 

 It may be stated here that in the written objection, in paragraph 6, the opposite party has stated that the petitioner's statement of giving land in borga appears to be fraudulent. That the petitioner is a co-sharer of the holding is a finding of fact which has been concluded by the concurrent findings of the courts below. However, since the opposite party has denied in a manner that the petitioner used to cultivate the land of his share in borga as alleged, the denial has given rise to an issue as to whether the petitioner used to cultivate his share through borgadar alleged and as such whether he was a bonafide cultivator. The courts below do not appear to have recorded any finding on this issue. It, however, does not appear from the Judgments of the courts below that this point was raised before them. Be that as it may, I find from the record that both the parties have adduced evidence on this point. On the evidence on record this court can decide the matter on merits. In this connection I would like to refer to A.I.R. 1931 (Lah) 748 where it was held that in a case of this nature wan open to the court to go through the record itself and decide the case on merits. I have already referred to the pleadings of the parties on thin point. Now referring to the evidence, it is found that the petitions P.W.1. Oziullah has stated in his examination-in chief that he gave takid for borga crop to his borgadar Nurul Amin. It has been brought out from his cross examination that in 1970 the borgadar delivered him borga paddy. P.W. 2 Abdur Rahim has stated that the petitioner has demanded borga paddy from Nurul Amin in his presence. O.P. No. I who deposed as O. P. No, 1 has, of course, denied the petitioner's story of borga to Nurul Amin or anybody else. Considering the evidence of both the parties in thin case, and considering the fact this issue does not at all appear to have been raised in the courts below, I feel no hesitation to hold that the petitioner used to cultivate the land of his share of the case-holding through borgadar and as such he is a bonafide cultivator. The failure of the courts below to record a finding that the petitioner is a bonafide cultivator is an irregularity but I have been fully satisfied after a consideration of the evidence on record that this omission to record a finding has not caused any failure of justice. Both the courts below have found that the petitioner was a person who was entitled to pre-empt and I find no reason to hold otherwise. There is no cause for interference.
